about: Side topic X5 (How are big energy projects actually financed?): a capital-stack builder for one wind and storage project, closed form. The project is Prairie Town's wind farm (town.json, illustrative) with lesson A2's battery; their building costs, upkeep and output come from lessons 7 and 13 and A2's data files, and the contract price from A1's, read through x05-inputs.json (the finance-only projection of those files, written by the X5 test). Every dollar is a 2025 dollar. The lender's settings below are illustrative values inside the dated ranges of the sources. One typical year stands for every year of the loan: no inflation, taxes, depreciation, construction loans, reserve accounts or tax-equity flip.

lender.rateNote: 6.5% a year, the toy's chosen rate: the 2025 ATB's nominal term-debt rate for land-based wind, utility solar and batteries. The toy has no inflation, so it uses that rate as it is (simplified).
lender.termNote: 15 years, illustrative: the battery's life in lesson 13's data. The 2025 ATB amortizes its loans over 18 years.
lender.dscrNote: Illustrative: the lender asks 1.30 times the loan payment from contracted cash and 2.00 times from cash sold at market prices. The 2025 ATB assumes minimum coverage ratios from 1.275 (utility solar) to 2.0 (utility batteries).

contract.note: Contracted: the wind output sold at A1's fixed price, as generated, under a [[power-purchase-agreement|power purchase agreement]], and the battery rented out under a [[tolling-agreement|tolling agreement]]. Merchant: market prices, the same on average (illustrative).

bad.note: A bad year, illustrative: 10% less wind and market prices 40% lower. A contract fixes the price, not the wind.

taxEquity.note: Tax equity needs a federal tax credit, which for wind depends on its dates under the 2025 law (lesson A12).

grant.note: A grant is public money that is not paid back, under its program's rules.

structure: This example assumes project-level debt, paid before either equity investor: operating costs first, then the loan, then tax equity, then the sponsor. Other deal structures order the cash differently.

layers.label: Sponsor equity
layers.who: The developer or owner: its own money.
layers.gets: What is left after everyone else; often the highest return asked.
layers.paid: Last: the first to lose when cash falls short.

layers.label: Tax equity
layers.who: Large firms with tax bills to cut, such as banks and insurers.
layers.gets: Most of the tax credits (cuts to its own tax bill) and the tax deductions for the equipment's wear (depreciation), plus some cash.
layers.paid: After the loan and ahead of the sponsor, on terms set in advance; it carries less risk than sponsor equity.

layers.label: Senior debt
layers.gets: Fixed loan payments: interest, plus repayment of the amount borrowed (the principal).
layers.paid: First, right after operating costs; the project's assets pledged as security (collateral) and rules the borrower must follow (covenants) protect it, so it asks the lowest return.

layers.label: Grant
layers.who: A public program, for example DOE's program for communities of 10,000 people or fewer.
layers.gets: Nothing back in cash; the project meets the program's conditions.
layers.paid: Never: it lowers what everyone else must put in.

risks.q: A bad year: cash falls short of what everyone expected. Who loses money first?

feedback.debt: Not first: in this example the loan is paid right after operating costs, before any owner gets cash.
feedback.te: Not first: tax equity is paid ahead of the sponsor on terms set in advance.
feedback.sponsor: Yes: the sponsor is paid last, so its share absorbs a shortfall first.

facts.what: Minimum debt-service coverage ratios the 2025 ATB assumes: 1.275 utility solar, 1.375 land-based wind, 1.45 gas, 2.0 utility batteries.
Share of a wind project's capital that tax equity typically provided where federal tax credits applied (2017).
Of the new U.S. wind capacity of 2023: at least 48% sold to direct retail buyers (corporations among them), 29% bought or owned by utilities, at least 9% merchant or quasi-merchant.
Estimated regional wholesale market value of wind output in 2023, from SPP to CAISO, in 2023 dollars; one project's receipts depend on its contracts and market arrangements.

deflator.note: GDP implicit price deflator (2017 = 100), annual: a 2023 dollar is 128.893 ÷ 122.451 2025 dollars.

stop.title: This side topic stops at the capital stack
stop.lede: Finance enters the course as who puts in money, who is paid first and why lenders value contracts; structuring deals is a profession of its own.
includes: The four layers of a capital stack and the order in which they are paid.
How a lender sizes a loan from cash flow and a coverage ratio.
Why contracted revenue supports more debt than revenue sold at market prices.
leaves: Structuring a deal: partnership flips, back-leverage, reserve accounts, term sheets.
Tax law, eligibility for credits and accounting standards.
Investment advice: this lesson rates no project and no investor.
